# Blueprint

> Get repetitive work done by robots. A site films one job that repeats, once. Blueprint builds a simulation of the site and sends the job, as a job packet (what the job is, a first look at which robots could fit, and the simulation of the site), to the robot deployment companies it approves, so they can test it and tell the site if they can do it. A site's name and contact details go to a company only when the site asks for an introduction. Free for sites.

The job packet holds the site's own sentence for the job, a first look on paper (the robot most likely to fit, from published specifications and where it has been used), a simulation of the site built from its video, and what counts as done. Sometimes Blueprint also tries openly available robot software on the job in that simulation; this is labelled an early trial, it is not the site's answer, and it does not predict what a deployment company's robot would do. A zero is a valid result of the trial. Some jobs are held when Blueprint can't build a simulation for that kind of job yet; the first look stays on the job page.

Blueprint shares each job with the deployment companies it approves by hand. Each job comes as a job packet: the site's description of the job, its video without sound, a first look at which robots could fit, the simulation of the site, what counts as done, and our early trial's result where one exists. A company can say it is interested, that the job is not a fit, or that it would need something; Blueprint can't promise any will say yes. When a company is interested, the site can ask for an introduction, and each gets the other's contact details. Any work is agreed between the site and the company. Nothing is charged today. A simulation is a bounded estimate and never certifies physical performance or safety.

Deployment companies apply on the page for deployment companies. Applications stay pending until Blueprint approves the company by hand; applying does not grant access or promise a job. Contact: hello@tryblueprint.io.

## Evidence boundary

Customer wording uses “job” for the work a site wants automated and “task” for the specific robot action and its technical conditions. API fields and identifiers retain their existing names.

A Task Evaluation Run returns a decision or abstention. Pipeline owns method qualification and routing; physical outcomes remain distinct from simulation and generated evidence.
